longQuestions: A pointer is a variable that holds the memory address of another variable of a given type, declared as type *name; e.g. int *p = &x;

Advantages: allow direct access and manipulation of memory; let functions change the caller's variables (pass by address) and return more than one value; make array and string handling efficient; are required for dynamic memory allocation (new/delete); allow building data structures such as linked lists and trees; can save memory and increase speed.
The reference (address-of) operator & gives the memory address of a variable; the dereference operator * gives the value stored at the address held by a pointer.

int x = 25;
int *p = &x;        // & : p gets the address of x
cout << p;          // prints an address, e.g. 0x7ffd5c
cout << *p;         // * : prints 25, the value at that address
*p = 40;            // changes x to 40 through the pointer
Pointer initialization means assigning an address to a pointer at the time of its declaration, so it does not hold a garbage address.
An ordinary variable declaration reserves memory to store a data value: int a; — a holds an integer value.

A pointer declaration uses an asterisk (*) before the name: int *p; — p holds the address of an integer variable, not an integer value. The data type of a pointer is the type of variable it points to, and it is given an address with &: p = &a;
